en: Recent work makes GED faster or replaces it with a learned score. Kim [n1] computes GED more efficiently by using isomorphic vertices, and Moscatelli et al. [n2] study node matching for edit distance. Moscatelli et al. [n3] predict GED with the Edges network, which turns the quadratic assignment problem into edge prediction on a GED instance graph and outputs a soft assignment matrix without a matching solver. Wang et al. [n4] and Chen et al. [n5] learn graph similarity with matching networks; GMN-Zoomer [n5] matches graphs at several levels of a hierarchy and fuses the results into one score. These models are trained with gradients and return a score or a soft assignment, so they do not show which edit led a classifier to a wrong class.

Prototype and concept models explain their decisions by design. PIP-PACA [n6] links image parts to prototypes and adds clustering attention between the prototypes. Proto-Caps [n7] explains medical image decisions with visual prototypes of appearance features that experts define in advance. Mbiaya et al. [n8] add a knowledge graph to a concept-based classifier to improve its accuracy. Vasu et al. [n9] build global concept-based explanations for any image classifier. Zhang et al. [n10] compute concept-based counterfactual explanations in closed form, and in their user study, participants identified model failures with 89.88% accuracy. Liu et al. [n24] form global prototypes for few-shot learning by training base and novel classes together. In all these works, the prototypes and concepts are learned or explained inside a network trained by gradient descent, and none of them records when a prototype or concept stops changing during training.

Brown et al. [n11] propose shortcut testing, a multitask method that checks whether a clinical model relies on improper correlations, and apply it in radiology and dermatology. Fay et al. [n15] split the image features into the primary task and a spuriously correlated factor and minimize the mutual information between them, so the network learns without the shortcut. Borges [n12] audits shortcut learning in breast cancer subtyping: one clinical predictor is changed at a time, and the shift of the predicted subtype probabilities shows which feature drives the misclassification. These studies detect or suppress shortcuts in a trained model as a whole or in its input features; they do not localize a wrong answer to a processing step.

Xie et al. [n18] model handwritten mathematical expressions as stroke graphs and label their nodes and edges with an edge-weighted graph attention network. The graph makes the structure of the expression explicit, but the network that labels it is trained end to end with gradients.

Several recent methods train without backpropagation. Forward Projection [n19] trains each layer in closed form with a single forward pass and no feedback from later layers. Nimmo and Mondragón [n20] build Hebbian convolutional networks with winner-takes-all competition, lateral inhibition and the Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro rule. Lin et al. [n21] study overfitting and anti-Hebbian learning in unsupervised Hebbian networks. Radhakrishnan et al. [n22] show that the average gradient outer product, which needs no backpropagation, describes feature learning in neural networks and lets kernel machines learn features. Xu et al. [n23] reformulate the Forward-Forward algorithm as distance metric learning to improve local learning. These methods remove backpropagation, but they still store what they learn in weights, not in a class structure that can be read.

In summary, graph matching studies measure distance, interpretability studies set requirements or explain trained models, error analysis examines models from outside, skeleton studies stop before the classification decision, and backpropagation-free methods still keep what they learn in weights. Yet we found no study that measured when the concept graphs of a structural classifier trained without gradients stop changing, or split all of its wrong-class answers by the decision step that caused them.

Software used: Python 3.12 (https://www.python.org), OpenCV 4.13 (https://opencv.org) (image reading), NetworkX 3.6 [25], scikit-image 0.26 [26], skan 0.13 [27], rdp 0.8 [28], Numba 0.64 [29]. Services run on Nuclio (https://github.com/nuclio/nuclio) + Kafka (https://kafka.apache.org), and graphs are stored in Neo4j (https://neo4j.com). The code is available at https://github.com/NaturalAGI-Lab/NaturalAGI [33].
